title: How to diagnose high CPU usage: thread dump (`jstack`), look for threads in RUNNABLE state doing heavy computation or infinite loops, or excessive GC (check GC logs)?
shortTitle: How do you diagnose high CPU usage?

s1_definition.oneliner: Find the hottest threads with top, take a jstack dump, match the hot native thread IDs to Java stacks, and rule out excessive GC via the GC logs.
s1_definition.profdef: Diagnosing high CPU in a Java process means identifying which threads are burning CPU and what code they are running. The standard technique is to find the operating-system threads consuming the most CPU, convert their native thread IDs to hexadecimal, take a thread dump with `jstack`, and match the hot native IDs to Java threads. Threads stuck in the RUNNABLE state doing heavy computation or spinning in an infinite loop are the usual culprits. The other major cause is excessive garbage collection, which you confirm by reading GC logs to see if GC threads are eating the CPU.

sections.s2_detail:
### What is diagnose high CPU usage?

The reliable method links operating-system CPU usage to a specific Java thread. On Linux you run `top -H -p <pid>` to show per-thread CPU for the Java process. You note the thread IDs (TIDs) burning the most CPU. Those are decimal native IDs. You convert each to hexadecimal, because a Java thread dump records the native id in hex under `nid=`. Then you take a thread dump with `jstack <pid>` and search for the matching `nid=0x...`. The stack trace at that thread tells you exactly which Java method is running hot.

### How does diagnose high CPU usage work?

A thread in the RUNNABLE state in the dump is actively using CPU (or ready to). If you see the same RUNNABLE stack across several dumps taken a few seconds apart, and it is deep inside a computation or a loop, that is your hotspot. A classic finding is an infinite or near-infinite loop – for example a `while` loop whose exit condition is never met, or a spin on a flag without a sleep. Another common finding is an unexpectedly expensive operation inside a hot path, like a regular expression with catastrophic backtracking or repeated string building.

### Why does this matter?

The second major cause of high CPU is excessive garbage collection. If the application threads are not obviously hot but CPU is pinned, the GC threads may be the ones working. You confirm this by reading GC logs (`-Xlog:gc`): if GC is running almost continuously and total GC time is a large fraction of uptime, the CPU is going into collection, usually because the heap is too small, there is a leak, or allocation is far too high. In a thread dump, GC threads show as JVM-internal threads, and tools like JFR or `jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000` make the GC-bound situation obvious.

### How do you use this in practice?

A senior nuance: take several thread dumps a few seconds apart rather than one, because a single dump is a snapshot that might catch a thread mid-normal-work. The hotspot is the stack that keeps appearing. Also distinguish user CPU (your code or GC computing) from system CPU (often heavy I/O or context switching). For deeper analysis, async-profiler's CPU flame graph pinpoints the hot method without the manual TID matching. And always profile under the real load that triggers the problem.

### What are the rules and constraints?

This aspect of diagnose high CPU usage is important for banking applications at National Bank of India. Rajesh regularly considers this when designing transaction processing systems.
sections.s6_takeaway:
When a Java process pegs the CPU, I do not guess; I link the operating system's view of CPU to a specific Java thread and the exact line it is running. On Linux I run top with the per-thread flag on the process id to see which thread is burning the most CPU, I note that thread's decimal id, and I convert it to hexadecimal, because a Java thread dump records the native id in hex. Then I take a thread dump with jstack and search for that hex id, and the stack trace right there tells me precisely which method is hot. A thread that is in the RUNNABLE state and sitting in the same deep computation or loop across two dumps taken a few seconds apart is my hotspot, and the classic finding is an infinite or spinning loop with no backoff, or an unexpectedly expensive operation like a regex with catastrophic backtracking.

The second thing I always check is whether the CPU is actually going into garbage collection rather than my own code. If no application thread looks busy but the CPU is still pinned, the GC threads are probably the ones working. I confirm that by reading the GC logs or running jstat to watch the GC time percentage, and if GC is running almost continuously the real problem is a heap that is too small, a memory leak, or an allocation rate that is far too high. I take several dumps rather than one, because a single snapshot can mislead, and for the fastest answer I use an async-profiler CPU flame graph, where the widest box is immediately the hot method with no manual id matching.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, this procedure solved two very different incidents. In one, our fraud-check service pinned a CPU core, and the thread dump showed a thread stuck RUNNABLE in a retry loop that spun on a condition that was never true with no backoff, so we fixed it by adding a proper wait and bounded retries. In another, the CPU was pinned but no application thread looked busy, and the GC logs revealed collection running nonstop because the heap was undersized for the load, so the fix was sizing the heap correctly rather than touching any application code. Knowing to separate an application hotspot from a GC-bound situation is what lets me fix the right thing fast under production pressure.

Remember one sentence: How to diagnose high CPU usage: thread dump (`jstack`), look for threads in RUNNABLE state doing heavy computation or infinite loops, or excessive GC (check GC logs) is fundamental knowledge for Java interviews and production banking work.

keyPoints: top -H -p PID: find the thread consuming CPU
Convert thread ID to hex: printf "%x" TID
jstack PID: thread dump – find the hex TID in the output
Common causes: infinite loop, busy-wait, excessive GC, regex backtracking
JFR CPU profiling shows exactly which methods consume the most CPU
